extracted.intended_audience: registered practitioners before the USPTO (patent agents and patent attorneys), and practitioners considering or receiving inventor referrals from non-practitioner third parties
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and disciplinary standards for USPTO registered practitioners who provide patent legal services to inventors referred by non-practitioner third parties (e.g., marketing/assistance companies). Covers conflicts, communication obligations, fee-sharing, unauthorized practice, and related sanctions and reinstatement conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the representation and basis of a fee (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must advise clients at the outset of the representation of the scope of the representation and the basis or rate of the fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to advise inventor-clients of the scope of representation and fee basis violates § 11.105(b). Practitioners should communicate what services will be provided (e.g., preparing vs. prosecuting an application) and what fees/expenses the client will be responsible for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed consent where responsibilities materially limited (37 C.F.R. § 11.107(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must obtain informed consent when the practitioner's responsibilities are materially limited due to a conflict of interest (e.g., financial interest in referrals from a third party).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must identify actual or potential conflicts (including conflicts arising from referral relationships or financial interests) and obtain informed consent after communicating adequate information and explanation about material risks and reasonably available alternatives. The mere fact that a client authorizes a third party to pay the practitioner is not sufficient for informed consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain a matter to permit informed client decisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include explaining: the practical effect of filing an international (PCT) application (that favorable ISA opinion does not create automatic international protection and additional national prosecution costs will be required), the 12‑month expiry of provisional applications, and whether to claim priority to a provisional when filing a later utility application. Failing to explain such material risks and alternatives violates § 11.104(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interference with independent professional judgment (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f)(2) and § 11.504(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not allow a person who pays the practitioner to direct or regulate the practitioner's professional judgment in rendering legal services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a referring company or payer instructs the practitioner not to communicate with clients or directs which types of applications to file, the practitioner may have allowed improper interference with independent judgment and thus violated § 11.108(f)(2) and § 11.504(c). Practitioners must independently determine appropriate patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abide by client's decisions and reasonably consult about means (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.102(a) and 11.104(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner must abide by the client's decisions concerning the objectives of representation and must reasonably consult with the client about the means by which those objectives are to be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must involve clients in decisions about objectives and strategy rather than passively following third‑party instructions; failing to consult about means constitutes a violation of §§ 11.102(a) and 11.104(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the client reasonably informed of status (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must keep the client reasonably informed about the status of a matter, including promptly informing the client of Office correspondence and critical deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failing this duty include not notifying clients that their provisional applications were about to expire or not informing clients of Office actions or correspondence. This violates § 11.104(a)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on assisting unauthorized practice / forming partnerships with non-practitioners (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.505 and 11.504(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not assist a non-practitioner to practice before the Office in violation of applicable law, and may not form a partnership with a non-practitioner if any of the partnership's activities consist of the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a non-practitioner company is engaging in activities that constitute practice before the Office (e.g., advising inventors about filing strategy, inserting signed documents into files, handling substantive client communications), the practitioner who accepts referrals and passively fills orders may be assisting unauthorized practice or forming a de facto partnership, violating § 11.505 and § 11.504(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise independent professional judgment and render candid advice (37 C.F.R. § 11.201)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must exercise independent professional judgment and render candid advice to clients, rather than merely rubber-stamping third-party recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent judgment includes assessing whether requested patent protection is appropriate, advising clients of alternatives and risks, and not sharing legal fees with non-practitioners (§ 11.504(a)). Practitioners are expected to inquire into amounts charged by referring third parties to ensure fees are not impermissibly shared and to ensure any undistributed compensation is returned to the inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify documents and materials exchanged by third-party referrers
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner receives referrals from a non-practitioner third party, the practitioner should obtain copies of all documents exchanged between the company and the inventor so the practitioner can determine whether the company is engaging in practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtaining these documents helps a practitioner determine whether the third party is doing tasks that may constitute the unauthorized practice of law or that affect conflicts/fee issues. Failure to obtain and review such materials may expose the practitioner to discipline for assisting unauthorized practice or forming a de facto partnership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee-sharing prohibition and duties regarding third-party compensation (37 C.F.R. § 11.504(a) and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not share legal fees with a non-practitioner; practitioners should be aware that receiving compensation indirectly via a referring third party can create impermissible fee sharing if amounts are not fully remitted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should carefully question inventors and the referring third-party about amounts charged and how funds are distributed. If the third party retains undistributed compensation and does not return it to the inventor, the practitioner has likely impermissibly shared fees. Practitioners must avoid arrangements that effectively split fees with non-practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and requirements for informed consent (as applied under USPTO rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informed consent requires that the client agree to representation after the practitioner has communicated adequate information and explanation about the material risks of and reasonably available alternatives to the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A meaningful discussion between practitioner and client is necessary for informed consent, particularly where a third party will pay the practitioner or where the practitioner's responsibilities are materially limited. Merely having the inventor authorize third-party payment is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical communication obligations when clients are referred (general guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inventor is referred by a non-practitioner, the practitioner's communications with that inventor should be no different in scope or substance from communications with clients who directly engaged the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must consult reasonably on means, keep inventors informed, and explain matters sufficiently to permit informed decisions. Delegating substantive client communication to subordinates or third parties without appropriate involvement may raise ethical concerns. Reliance on a bona fide corporate liaison or foreign agent to convey instructions is permissible only with client consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, reinstatement conditions, and publication of disciplinary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary remedies and procedural conditions imposed by the USPTO in this matter: suspension, eligibility to petition for reinstatement, exam and score requirements, probation, and publication of the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative terms from this Final Order: 20‑month suspension from practice; eligibility to petition for reinstatement after 18 months but no reinstatement before full 20‑month suspension; as a condition of reinstatement, take the MPRE and attain a score of 85 or better and provide corroborating declaration(s); 28‑month probation commencing upon reinstatement; limited recognition for 30 days to facilitate compliance; OED may issue an Order to Show Cause and seek additional suspension (up to 16 months) for violations during probation; Final Order to be published in OED Reading Room and Official Gazette. Nothing prevents OED from using this record in future proceedings.
